newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader wants union, not merger with Russia.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader wants union, not merger with Russia.

text.p: Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko said on Wednesday that he and Russian President Boris Yeltsin would iron out differences over a union charter between their two countries.

But, on the eve of his departure for Moscow to meet Yeltsin and sign the union charter, he ruled out creation of a federation with Russia and said media speculation on that issue was a provocation intended to torpedo the union.

"Setting up a federation with Russia would be worse for Belarus than when it entered (Soviet dictator Josef) Stalin's Soviet Union," Lukashenko told reporters. "We were not part of Russia under the Soviet Union."
Yeltsin and Lukashenko are due to meet in Moscow on Thursday and plan to sign the charter, deepening integration between their two former Soviet republics, the following day.
They signed an outline union agreement in Moscow on April 2 but left the guts of the treaty, including the more controversial points, to be put in the separate charter.
The union charter now appears to satisfy Lukashenko less than the original draft, which was watered down by Kremlin liberals.

Many Russians and Belarussians, nostalgic for the Soviet Union which collapsed more than five years ago, support the idea of union between the Russian Federation of 150 million people and its western Slav neighbour of only 10 million.
Yeltsin has said a complete merger of the two countries is his ultimate goal, but Lukashenko says he wants a union of two equal sovereign states.
The Kremlin said on Tuesday there were still some obstacles blocking the charter but that Yeltsin expected to overcome them in time to sign the document.
Lukashenko said the remaining questions to be settled were the powers of union governing bodies, the powers of the chairman of the union's supreme concil and the location of the bodies.
He also said a single currency and army could not be created immediately and required a referendum.
"The constitutions of our two countries do not allow that. This may be changed only through a referendum," he said.
